To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) we propose a novel estimator for learning Ising models that is computationally tractable and requires a number sampling complexity that is near-optimum; (ii) we prove that the estimator is consistent and that with appropriate regularization recovers the underlying Ising model; (iii) our results have implications in statistical mechanics and machine learning; (iv) the estimator can be implemented in polynomial time using a convex program and is robust to the presence of noise.

we have developed an efficient and sample-efficient estimator that can be used to learn the underlying graph of a p-spin Ising model from samples, and that the estimator has a physical explanation that is related to the concept of interaction screening.
we provide an algorithm that learns the Ising model with near-optimal sample complexity.

the interaction screening estimator is a sample-optimal, computationally efficient, convex estimator for learning the underlying graph in an Ising model.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we provide an algorithm that is both computationally efficient and sample-optimal.
we have proposed a new statistical learning problem and have developed an efficient estimator that achieves near-optimal sample complexity.
we provide a sample-optimal algorithm for the Ising model, and we provide a new estimator that has a physical interpretation and can be efficiently implemented.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is possible to efficiently learn an Ising model from a sample of size that is near-optimum, even when the underlying graph is dense.
for Ising models on sparse graphs, the number of samples required to recover the underlying graph scales as O(p log p) with high probability.

, for the Ising model, the number of samples required to recover the underlying graph scales exponentially in its complexity (as measured by the maximum coupling-intrength and the maximum degree of a node) rather than linearly as in the classical case of learning the underlying structure of a Markov random field.
